notes.meaning: Judas Maccabeus began this winter festival to remember the cleansing and restoring of the temple after an enemy defiled it. It lasted eight days in the cold month of December. Even though this feast was not commanded in the law of Moses, Jesus came to Jerusalem during it to teach the crowds.

Jesus walked in a covered walkway along the east side of the temple courts. This colonnade provided shelter from the cold and stormy winter weather. It kept the name of Solomon because it stood in the same place where Solomon's original temple porch had once stood.

The Jewish leaders gathered tightly around Jesus and demanded to know if He was the Messiah. They claimed He was keeping them in painful suspense. In truth, they were not looking to learn, but hoped to trap Him into words that could be used against Him before the Roman rulers.

Jesus answered that He had already told them who He was, but they refused to trust Him. His miracles and healing deeds were done in His Father's name and gave open proof of His identity. The fault was not a lack of plain evidence, but their own stubborn refusal to believe.

The leaders did not refuse to believe because Christ's message was dark or confusing. They did not believe because they did not belong to His flock. Their proud and stubborn hearts showed that they were not ready to follow Him as gentle and teachable sheep.

Jesus described the true mark of those who belong to Him. His sheep listen to His voice and recognize His call. He knows and cares for each one personally, and they respond by following Him in daily obedience.

Jesus freely gives His followers eternal life, a gift that begins right now and never ends. He promises that they will never perish in final ruin. Because they are held in His mighty hand, no enemy or robber has the power to tear them away.

differ.view: Reformed Christians believe true believers are securely kept by Christ and can never fall away or lose their eternal salvation.
Methodists believe believers remain secure only as long as they continue in faith and obedience to Christ.
Some Anglicans hold that while no outside force can snatch believers away, they retain free will and may choose to depart.

notes.meaning: Jesus pointed to His Father, who gave these sheep to Him, as greater and more powerful than all creation. Because the Father holds them just as tightly, no foe on earth or in hell can snatch them from His grasp. The safety of the sheep rests upon the supreme strength of God Himself.

Jesus declared that He and the Father are one. This means they are not one single person, but one in nature, power, and purpose. In saving and keeping the sheep, the Son shares the very same divine strength and dignity as the Father.

The hearers understood exactly what Jesus was saying, so they picked up heavy stones to kill Him. Under Jewish law, speaking evil against God or claiming His divine rights was punished by stoning. Their sudden fury proved that they knew He was claiming to be God.

Jesus answered their anger with gentle and piercing words. He asked them which of His many kind deeds—curing the sick, giving sight to the blind, and helping the poor—had earned their hatred. Every good work He showed them had come directly from the Father's kindness.

The leaders insisted they were not stoning Him for any act of kindness, but for blasphemy, which means insulting the honor of God. In their eyes, Jesus was merely an ordinary mortal man who was daring to make Himself God. Because they refused to see His divine nature in His works, they treated His words as a terrible sin.

Jesus pointed them back to Psalm 82 in their own Scriptures, where God addressed human judges and rulers as 'gods.' Those rulers were given that title because they sat in God's place to carry out justice for the nation. Jesus met His accusers on their own holy ground to silence their charge.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some Word of Faith teachers use this verse to claim that Christians are little gods who can speak things into reality.

notes.meaning: Jesus reminded them that Scripture cannot be set aside, broken, or proved wrong. If God's inspired word applied the title of gods to mortal men who merely received His command, that language cannot be called unlawful. His argument reasoned from the lesser human judges to the far greater One.

Jesus showed how unreasonable their charge was. If earthly judges could be called gods, how could they accuse the One whom the Father set apart and sent into the world of blasphemy for saying, 'I am the Son of God?' He held a sacred commission that far surpassed any human ruler.

Jesus offered a fair and simple test for His claims. If He was not performing the mighty works that belong to God the Father alone, they had no need to believe Him. He never asked for blind trust without giving clear proof of who He was.

Even if the leaders refused to trust His words alone, Jesus urged them to consider the evidence of His miracles. Those works clearly showed that the Father was dwelling and acting in Him, and that He was in the Father. Observing the works would help them understand that He and the Father share the same power and life.

Instead of being softened by His reasoning, the leaders tried to grab Him so they could punish Him. Yet Jesus slipped freely out of their hands by His divine power. He did not run away out of fear, but because the right time for Him to give His life on the cross had not yet arrived.

Jesus walked away from Jerusalem and crossed over the Jordan River. He stayed in the rural area where John the Baptist had carried out his early ministry of baptizing. There, away from the plotting leaders, He found a quiet place to continue His work.

Many people traveled to see Jesus and remembered what John the Baptist had preached in that very valley. They recognized that while John had never worked a miracle, everything he had said about Jesus was entirely true. John's past teaching had prepared their hearts to welcome Christ.

Many people in that countryside believed in Jesus and put their trust in Him. While Jerusalem's proud leaders had rejected Him with stones, these humble listeners received Him as the true Messiah. God's truth bore rich fruit where John's message had paved the way.
